title: Lecture 1: Vectors and Spaces
notes: Three perspectives on vectors: physics (arrow with length and direction), CS (ordered list of numbers), and math (generalized vector space).
Vector addition as head-to-tail geometric displacement.
Scalar multiplication as stretching or squishing coordinate lengths.

transcript.text: What is a vector? In linear algebra, vectors are both arrows in geometric space and lists of numerical features.
When we add two vectors, we place them head-to-tail and draw an arrow from start to finish.
Multiplying by a scalar scales the length and flips direction if negative.

title: Lecture 2: Linear Combinations, Span, and Basis Vectors
notes: Standard basis vectors i-hat and j-hat.
Linear combinations: scaling basis vectors and adding them.
Span: the set of all possible vectors reachable by linear combinations.
Linear independence: when adding a vector increases the dimensionality of the span.

transcript.text: The span of a set of vectors is the entire subspace you can reach using linear combinations.
Two linearly independent 2D vectors span the entire 2D plane.
Basis vectors form a minimal set that spans the space without redundancy.

title: Lecture 3: Linear Transformations and Matrices
notes: A transformation is linear if grid lines remain parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin remains fixed.
A linear transformation is completely determined by where it sends the basis vectors i-hat and j-hat.
Packaging the landing coordinates of basis vectors into matrix columns.

transcript.text: Linear transformations are functions that take in vectors and output transformed vectors while keeping lines parallel and origin fixed.
To describe any 2D linear transformation, you only need to know where i-hat and j-hat land.
Those two landing points become the two columns of a 2 by 2 matrix.

title: Lecture 4: Linear Transformations as Matrix-Vector Products
notes: Computing A * x: scaling columns of A by coordinates of x and adding.
Rotations, shears, and reflections represented as 2x2 matrices.
Geometric intuition behind matrix multiplication formulas.

transcript.text: Matrix-vector multiplication is simply computing a linear combination of the matrix's columns.
Rotating the plane 90 degrees sends i-hat to (0, 1) and j-hat to (-1, 0).
Multiplying any vector [x, y] by this matrix yields its rotated coordinates.

title: Lecture 5: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Transformations
notes: Multiplying matrices A * B corresponds to applying transformation B first, followed by A.
Matrix multiplication is associative: A * (B * C) = (A * B) * C.
Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative: A * B != B * A in general.

transcript.text: Why is matrix multiplication defined the way it is? Because it represents composition of transformations.
Applying a rotation followed by a shear is not the same as shearing first and rotating second.
Tracking where basis vectors land after sequential transformations derives the standard row-column rule.

title: Lecture 6: Vector Transformations in 2D and 3D
notes: Extending linear transformations to 3D: tracked by i-hat, j-hat, and k-hat.
3x3 matrices: columns represent landing coordinates in R^3.
Projections from 3D to 2D in computer graphics camera pipelines.

transcript.text: Moving from 2D to 3D: three basis vectors define 3x3 matrices with 9 parameters.
3D rotations along arbitrary axes and perspective projections.
Computer graphics engines use 4x4 homogeneous matrices to combine linear transformations and translations.

title: Lecture 7: Introduction to Matrices and Systems of Equations
notes: Translating systems of linear equations into matrix equation A * x = v.
Geometric interpretation: finding vector x that gets transformed into target v by matrix A.
Gaussian elimination and row echelon form.

transcript.text: Solving systems of simultaneous linear equations is equivalent to inverting a matrix transformation.
In A x = v, we are looking for the original vector x that lands on target v under transformation A.
If A doesn't squish space into a lower dimension, a unique inverse transformation exists.

title: Lecture 8: Determinants, Inverses, and Null Spaces
notes: The determinant measures how much a transformation scales areas (or volumes).
Sign of determinant: positive preserves orientation; negative reverses orientation.
A determinant of zero means space is squished into lower dimensions, meaning no inverse exists.
Null space / Kernel: set of all vectors that get squished onto the origin.

transcript.text: The determinant of a matrix tells you the factor by which area scales under the transformation.
If det(A) = 0, the transformation squishes the entire 2D plane onto a 1D line or point.
When det(A) is non-zero, A is invertible and A^(-1) undoes the transformation exactly.
